title: Boiling Point by Elevation Calculator
description: Estimate water's boiling point at any elevation with the Boiling Point by Elevation Calculator — standard-atmosphere physics, °C and °F. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, in Denver (1,609 m) water boils at about 94.7°C (202.4°F) — so eggs take longer, pasta sulks, and pressure cookers earn their keep in the Mile High City.
quick_answer: The Boiling Point by Elevation Calculator estimates the temperature at which water boils at a given elevation, using the standard atmosphere's pressure at that height. Enter the elevation and read the boiling point in Celsius and Fahrenheit — the number behind altitude cooking adjustments.
steps_intro: Lower pressure, lower boiling point — physics you can cook with:

body.t: Baking times, candy stages and egg timings all assume 100°C water. At 2,000 m your water is boiling near 93°C — recipes fail politely until you adjust — pressure first from the
At 3,640 m (La Paz) water boils at about 87.9°C: pasta stays stubborn, sterilising takes longer, and fuel budgets grow. The number plans the kitchen.
Strike temperatures and sterilisation protocols reference boiling; altitude labs recalibrate by exactly this curve.
Boiling is pressure's victory over vapour pressure — one curve of elevations makes the concept edible in a classroom.
At 8,849 m the boiling point falls to about 70.3°C (158.5°F) — too cool to brew proper tea or cook pasta through, which is why high camps melt snow and pressure-cook what they can.

Near sea level the boiling point drops about 1°C per 300 m of elevation (100.0°C → 96.7°C over the first kilometre, by this model). A cook's rule that happens to be physics, approximately — labelled as the approximation it is.

popular_table.title: Boiling point by elevation (standard atmosphere)
popular_table.intro: Computed from standard pressure via water's vapour-pressure curve.
popular_table.note: Values use the standard atmosphere; a strong high-pressure day raises your local boiling point slightly, a storm lowers it. Dissolved salts raise it too — seawater boils about 0.6°C hotter than fresh at sea level.

faq: Two physical steps: standard-atmosphere pressure at your elevation, then the temperature at which water's vapour pressure equals that pressure (the Antoine relation). Boiling is defined by the equality — the calculator just evaluates it.
Yes, slightly: real pressure wanders a few percent around standard with weather, moving the boiling point by a few tenths of a degree at low altitude. The standard value is the planning number.
Why do eggs take longer at altitude?
Because the water is cooler — 94.7°C in Denver cannot push heat into an egg like 100°C does. Time substitutes for temperature, within limits the recipe books tabulate.
By raising the pressure above atmospheric, the boiling point climbs back — a cooker at 15 psi adds roughly an atmosphere, restoring (and exceeding) sea-level boiling at any elevation.
Each liquid has its own vapour-pressure curve; this calculator is water's. Milk, oils and solvents each need their own relation.
Pressure rises, so boiling does too: at the Dead Sea shore (−430 m) water boils near 101.5°C by the same model.
